abstract: Target-based screening of covalent fragment libraries with mass spectrometry has emerged as a powerful strategy to identify chemical starting points for small molecule inhibitors or find new binding pockets on proteins of interest. These libraries span diverse chemical space with a modest number of compounds. Screening covalent fragments against purified protein targets reduces the demands on the mass spectrometer with respect to absolute throughput, detection limit, and dynamic range. Given these relaxed analytical requirements, we sought to develop an open-source, medium-throughput mass spectrometry system for target-based covalent fragment screening. Our platform comprises automated, dual LC desalting columns integrated with electrospray ionization for rapid sample introduction and mass spectrometry detection. The system is operated through a simple Python graphical user interface running on commodity microcontroller boards which allow integration with diverse liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry instruments. We provide scripts for fragment pooling, construction of sample batches, along with routines for data processing and visualization. The system enables primary screening of ~10,000 covalent fragments per day in pooled format. In a proof-of-concept study we executed primary and secondary screens to identify 27 hit fragments against UCHL1, a deubiquitinating enzyme that is emerging as a drug target of interest across multiple clinical indications. We validated and triaged these covalent compounds through a series of orthogonal biochemical and chemoproteomic assays. The most promising chloroacetamide covalent fragment inhibited UCHL1 activity in vitro (IC 50 < 5 μM) and exhibited dose-dependent binding along with good selectivity against 57 cellular DUBs as quantified by activity-based protein profiling.

Methods
2.1.
Open source hardware, electronics, and software
Instrument hardware was designed in Sketchup Pro (2024, Trimble;
Supplementary Fig. 1
). The frame consisted of OpenBuilds (
https://openbuildspartstore.com/
) aluminum V-slot assembled using T-nuts and brackets, with castors (Grainger) added for system mobility. Aluminum extrusion was cut to length according to the specifications using a residential grade compound miter saw and compatible non-ferrous metal blade. The 3-axis sample injector was based on an Openbuilds C-beam machine CNC system and assembled according to manufacturer instructions. Linear motion along X, Y, and Z axes was achieved with lead screw actuators each driven by a dedicated NEMA-23 stepper motor. The syringe pump was driven by a separate C-beam machine X-axis and NEMA-23 stepper motor. Each stepper motor was controlled with a DMT-542 stepper motor driver (
www.omc-stepperonline.com/
). The stepper motor drivers were controlled through Arduino-Unos loaded with grbl2arduino. One Arduino controlled the 3-axis autosampler gantry and a second Arduino-Uno controlled the syringe pump. A Python script (RobotControl.py) running on a Raspberry Pi controlled the Arduino-Unos as well as timing for contact closures for the system valve position (sample flow path control), LC (initiate organic gradient), and mass spectrometer (start acquisition). To organize and stabilize electronic connections amongst platform components, we designed (Autodesk Eagle) a custom printed circuit board (PCB, Osh Park) that accepted a 48 pin header from the Pi and routed 6-pin IDC connectors for each valve as well as a dedicated connection for each contact closure. We used wxPython to build a simple GUI for system control.
Supplementary Fig. 2
shows overall electronics layout, with a BOM provided in
Supplementary Table 1
. We provide PCB files, Open-SCAD files for 3D printed parts, and Python code as
Supplementary Material
.
2.2.
Model proteins
Cytochrome C (equine) and enolase (yeast) were obtained from Sigma. Proteins were dissolved in PBS and protein concentration was measured by BCA.
2.3.
UCHL1 expression and purification
GST-tag construct of full length human UCHL1 (residues 1–223; gift from Dr. Chunxiang Wu) was overexpressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) and purified using affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography. Briefly, cells were grown at 37 °C in TB medium in the presence of 100 μg/mL of ampicillin to an OD of 0.8, cooled to 17 °C, induced with 400 μM isopropyl-1-thio-D-galactopyranoside (IPTG), incubated overnight for 20 h at 17 °C, collected by centrifugation, and stored at −80 °C. Cell pellets were lysed in buffer A (25 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 5 % glycerol, and 0.5 mM TCEP) using Microfluidizer (Microfluidics), and the resulting lysate was centrifuged at 30,000 g for 40 min. Glutathione beads (GSH-sepharose, Cytiva) were mixed with cleared lysate for 90 min and washed with buffer A. Beads were transferred to an FPLC-compatible column, and the bound protein was washed further with buffer A for 10 column volumes and eluted with buffer B (25 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 5 % glycerol, 0.5 mM TCEP, and 15 mM glutathione). The eluted sample was concentrated and purified further using a Superdex 200 16/600 column (Cytiva) in buffer A. GST-3C protease was added to SEC fractions, containing GST-UCHL1, and incubate overnight at 4 °C. GST-tag was removed by applying to a second glutathione bead column and purified further using a Superdex 75 16/600 column (Cytiva) in buffer A. The eluant containing cleaved UCHL1 was concentrated to ~30 mg/mL and stored in −80 °C. UCHL3 was prepared similarly.
2.4.
Injection scheme and LC–MS
The system utilized a total of 5 valves to parallelize two sample flow paths.
Supplementary Fig. 3
shows the configuration of three low pressure, 6-port and two high pressure (one 6-port and one 10-port) valves. Proteins were eluted from each column with a 30-s HPLC gradient (
Supplementary Table 2
) that ramped from 0 to 100 % B in 24 s, followed by a linear ramp down to 0 % B in 6 s. We incorporated a 7 s delay to allow valve switching and pressure stabilization before launching the next gradient, for an inject-to-inject time of 37 s. Solvent A comprised 0.2 M acetic acid; solvent B comprised 60 % acetonitrile, 20 % isopropyl alcohol, 20 % n-propyl alcohol, and 0.2 M Acetic Acid. To inject the protein fragment samples, a 360 × 200 μm fused silica needle was positioned into the specified well and aspirated using the syringe actuator, placing the sample plug at the center of the 100 μL loop that spanned two ports of the 10-port valve. Actuating the 10-port valve placed the sample loop into the active flow path, and a single channel LC pump (Shizmadzu) pushed the sample plug onto one of the columns at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. Protein fragment samples were eluted from the column with a binary LC system (Shizmadzu). Between injections, the fused silica needle and flowpaths are rinsed with PBS that is collected into a waste container.
Supplementary Fig. 4
illustrates the interleaved injection scheme which runs repeatedly until all wells of the reaction plate are analyzed.
2.5.
Fragment screening
Covalent fragments were obtained from Enamine (Monmouth Jct., NJ, 3200 compounds, “Cysteine focused Covalent Fragments library CYS-3200-50-Y-20) and ChemDiv (San Diego, CA, 1000 compounds selected from “Cysteine Targeting Covalent Ligand Library” based on criteria listed in
Supplementary Methods
). Both vendors supplied csv files with compound identifiers, plate ID, well, smiles, MW, and warhead. Warheads were grouped according to their type using vendor specific designations. For example, Enamine labeled chloroacetamides as ’Covalent3 - ClAcAmide_base’ and ’Covalent2 - ClAcAmide_nobase’ whereas ChemDiv used ’CL_AC’. These groups were used by Create-ScreenPools.py to pool only compounds of similar warhead type, for example:

A liquid handler (i7, Beckman Coulter) was then used to pool equal volumes of ≤5 compounds based on the output CreateScreenPools.py using the Span-8 pipettor. For wells having <5 compounds, DMSO was added to keep concentrations and volumes the same. A total of 3 master pool plates were created, (1) acrylamides and cyanoacrylamides, (2) chloroacetamides and chloroketones, and (3) other. Dilutions of the 3 master pool plates were then produced using the 96-well pipetting head of the i7 liquid handler (384 wells accessed in quadrants i.e. upper left, upper right, lower left, lower right).
Screening reactions were performed by using the i7 to distribute UCHL1 from a quarter reservoir (20 mL capacity) across 3 × 384-well plates (1 μg per well, 40 μL, ~10 min. transfer time, span 8 probe) to match appropriately diluted pool plates (each of up to five compounds having a final concentration of 500 μM). We used the same platform to stamp 1 μL from 384 well dilution plates to corresponding wells of the protein plates. After 2 h, we used the liquid handler to quench each reaction well with 5 μL of 1 % formic acid, and mix. Plates were stored at −80 °C until analysis. Although less convenient, it should be noted that pooling, dilution, protein distribution, reactions, and quenching can also be performed manually with a 12-channel multichannel pipettor (odds, evens format). Sample lists were created for the mass spectrometer using ScreenPoolNamingWizard.py. User can select which screening plate is being interrogated, enter date, protein, datafile path, and MS method, and generate a csv file which can be imported into XCalibur software. Pool numbers are encoded into the datafile names for processing by FragmentScreen.py, which automated the analysis of the data files. This program utilizes Unidec [
41
] and the Multiplierz [
42
] toolkit to directly read and process native mass spectrometry data files to generate intact protein mass spectra along with an assessment of single-versus multi-covalent labeling and an estimate of fragment binding stoichiometry. FragmentScreen.py outputs graphically annotated PowerPoint slides to facilitate manual interpretation and figure generation, as well as a SQL file to support programmatic analysis or integration with other structure-based or chemi-informatic software tools. Scripts and auxiliary files are included in
Supplementary material
as Open-SourceHarwareSoftware.zip.
2.6.
Ubiquitin rhodamine 110 kinetic assay
The inhibitory activity of each covalent hit fragment on UCHL1 was evaluated using the ubiquitin rhodamine 110 kinetic assay. All assays were performed at 2 nM UCHL1 and 200 nM ubiquitin rhodamine 110 (Boston Biochem) in 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, and 0.02 % Tween20 in 384-well plates (Corning). The assay was initiated with the addition of ubiquitin rhodamine 110. Kinetic fluorescence data were collected every 30 s over a 30-min period (excitation and emission at 480 nm and 535 nm, respectively) on a BMG LABTECH CLARIOstar Microplate Reader. Initial velocities (RFU/min) were extracted and plotted against Log[fragment, μM]. IC
50
values were derived using GraphPad Prism (non-linear regression: log(inhibitor) vs. response (three parameters)). Initially, fragments were tested on an eight-point dose-response curve (3.13–200 μM) with a two-hour incubation with UCHL1 at room temperature, with the assay repeated two times for each fragment (
n
= 2). Inhibitory compounds were then re-analyzed with twelve-point dose-response curves (400 nM - 400 μM) each repeated four times (
n
= 4), except for Z203045204 which was re-analyzed over a range of 100 nM–600 μM (
n
= 4). SB-1-F22, “F22” is a positive control compound [
17
] and was analyzed over a range of 4 nM–4 μM.
2.7.
In vitro target engagement
UCHL1 protein in PBS was incubated with each covalent fragment at the indicated concentration for 2 h at room temperature and then coincubated with a 10-fold molar excess of ubiquitin activity probe (ABP; 1:1 mix of biotin-Ub-PA and biotin-Ub-VME; UbiQ, Amsterdam, Netherlands) for 2 h at room temperature. Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and visualized by Coomassie staining. Gels were imaged on a Bio Rad Gel Doc XR+ (white epi illumination, white light conversion screen, 60 s exposure). Signal for Ub-ABP bound UCHL1 relative to DMSO control was determined by densitometry with ImageJ software [
43
]. Blockage was calculated as 1-(signal treated ABP-UCHL1/signal DMSO ABP-UCHL1) × 100 %.
2.8.
Middle-down proteomics
UCHL1 (1 μg) was incubated with covalent fragment (typically 3–25 μM) for between 2 and 16 h. Protein–fragment reactions were diluted with an equal volume of 8 M urea/50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, treated with 100 ng endoproteinase AspN (Promega, Madison, WI) for ~15 min at 37C, and then quenched with 10 % formic acid. N-terminal and C-terminal fragments from UCHL1 were loaded on onto a self-packed column (5 cm 50R2 packed into 500 μm PEEK tubing) and eluted using an HPLC gradient (0–100 % B in 1 min, A = 0.2 M acetic acid, B = 0.2 M acetic acid in acetonitrile) and subjected to CID MS/MS on a 7600 Zeno-Tof mass spectrometer (AB-Sciex) with a spray voltage of 5.5 kV. The mass spectrometer acquired MS1 scans and targeted CID MS/MS scans for labeled peptides (CE typically 15–25 eV, unit resolution). 2.9.
UCHL1/UCHL3 mixed reaction assay
UCHL1 and UCHL3 (1 μg each) were mixed and diluted with PBS to a final concentration of 1 μM, reacted with indicated compounds for 2 h at room temperature, and analyzed by LC–MS. Stoichiometry of UCHL1 was assessed from the peak height of doubly labeled protein, as middle down MS experiments indicated the second labeling event occupied the catalytic cysteine.
2.10.
Spectral library construction
A DUB-specific spectral library was generated from several independent samples of ABPP-enriched DUBs (protocol below) using HEK293 cell extracts. Following trypsin digestion, the peptides were analyzed using an optimized data-independent acquisition method on a tims-TOF Flex2 instrument. The spectral library was generated in DIA-NN (1.8.2 beta 8) using a library-free approach. The following search parameters were used: MS1 accuracy: 15 ppm, MS2 accuracy: 10 ppm, fixed carbamidomethylation of cysteines (+57.02146), variable oxidation of methionines (+15.9949), variable modification of cysteines with the tryptic remnants of the ubiquitin vinyl ester and ubiquitin propargyl amide probes (+172.085, +112.064 respectively). N-terminus methionine excision was enabled along with unrestricted digestion C-terminal of arginine and lysine residues, allowing 2 missed cleavages. Additional parameters were specified as follows: minimum fragment
m/z
set to 200, maximum fragment
m/z
set to 1800, minimum peptide length set to 6, maximum peptide length set to 40, minimum precursor
m/z
set to 300, maximum precursor
m/z
set to 1800, minimum precursor charge set to 2 and maximum precursor charge set to 6. Library precursors were reannotated using a FASTA database of human sequences downloaded from UniProt on 2023-08-10 appended to common contaminants. Only spectral matches with a
q
-value <0.01 were retained.
2.11.
Activity-based protein profiling
Pellets of HEK293T cells were lysed with 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5 % NP-40, 10 % glycerol and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation (14,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C). Protein concentration was measured by BCA and aliquots of extract were treated with indicated compounds for 4 h at room temperature. An equal mixture of ubiquitin activity probes (ABP; Ub-PA/VME; 50 μM probe/mg protein; UbiQ, Amsterdam, Netherlands) was then added and allowed to react for 15 min at room temperature. Magnetic streptavidin beads (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA) were added to capture proteins bound by the ABP and washed with PBS/0.2 % SDS to reduce the level of non-specifically bound proteins. Enriched proteins were then eluted with hexafluoroisopropanol. Eluted proteins were digested on STRAP micro columns (Protifi, Long Island, NY) according to the manufacturer instructions. Peptides were loaded onto EVO tips (Odense, Denmark) according to the manufacturer instructions and analyzed with a 20-SPD method on an EVO Sep One (column = 75 μm I.D. packed with 15 cm 1.5 μm Dr. Maisch C18 [ESI Source Solutions, Woburn, MA] with integrated emitter tip [
44
]) coupled to a Bruker timsTOF Flex2 mass spectrometer operated in DIA mode. For each compound, triplicates of each treatment (0, 5, 10, and 25 μm) for 2 independent experiments were analyzed (
n
= 6). Data files were processed with DIA-NN version 1.8.2 beta 8 using a custom spectral library of DUBs (see ‘
Spectral Library Construction
’ above). Other DIA-NN search settings were the same as above, except that MS1 and MS2 mass accuracies were set to auto-inference. After filtering DIA-NN results for precursors with intensity >1000, differential abundance analysis was performed using MS-DAP [
45
], using default settings (
https://github.com/ftwkoopmans/msdap
) with filter_min_peptide_per_prot = 2, dea_qvalue_threshold =0.05, and diffdetect_min _peptides_observed = 3. Heat maps were generated with Python 3.12 and show values for blockage > 50 % and
q

1.
Introduction
Systematic studies spanning DNA sequencing, functional genomics, and integrated analysis of multi-omic data continue to highlight new targets in well-established druggable enzymes [
1
–
6
], as well as gene families such as the deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) that have more recently emerged as potential disease drivers [
7
–
9
]. There are approximately 100 human DUBs that catalyze cleavage of ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like (UBL) post-translational marks from substrate proteins [
10
]. As key members of the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), DUBs are functionally involved in numerous cellular processes. DUBs are classified into seven sub-families based on sequence homology with most functioning as cysteine proteases. The Ubiquitin Carboxy-Terminal Hydrolase L1 (UCHL1) is a small protein (~28 kDa) in the UCH sub-family [
11
]. UCHL1 is thought to stabilize the cellular pool of ubiquitin by binding free, monomeric ubiquitin, while also deubiquitinating other substrates, including endogenous peptides and metabolites. UCHL1 is very abundant in neuronal tissues, has limited expression in most other healthy tissues, but is over-expressed in several cancers. Accordingly, UCHL1 loss-of-function is linked to neurodegenerative disorders [
12
,
13
] while increased activity, primarily through increased protein abundance, is thought to play a role in multiple cancers [
14
].
Recent clinical success has driven renewed interest in covalent drugs [
15
,
16
]. Compared to their reversible counterparts, covalent inhibitors provide high efficacy at lower concentration and less frequent dosing, complete target inhibition, with activity restored only after
de novo
synthesis of new protein, and wider tolerance for pharmacokinetic parameters. Building on chemotypes reported in the patent literature [
17
], we [
18
] and others [
19
–
22
] have used complementary approaches to characterize diverse N-cyanopyrrolidines and chloroacetohydrazides as covalent inhibitors of UCHL1. Together, these studies establish the chemical tractability of UCHL1 for pharmacologic inhibition although the reported compounds performed unevenly with respect to their on- and off-target activity profiles. Collectively, these results inspired us to consider alternative approaches to diversify chemical starting points for UCHL1 inhibitory compounds.
Covalent fragment screening is gaining momentum as a powerful strategy to identify chemical starting points or find new binding pockets on protein targets [
23
–
29
]. Compared to diversity compound collections often used with traditional high-throughput screening (HTS) approaches, covalent fragments provide efficient coverage of chemical space with smaller libraries [
30
]. Irreversible binding driven by mild electrophile groups enables rigorous characterization of covalent modification by mass spectrometry with overall fragment activity profiles mediated by a balance of warhead reactivity and non-covalent interactions with the protein target. Recent advances now provide functionalized fragment libraries [
31
], to facilitate selectivity profiling and target deconvolution in complex proteomes, as well as covalent warheads that target other (e.g., non-cysteine) amino acids [
32
–
37
], thereby extending the reach of fragment screening. Use of purified protein and covalent compound libraries for target-based fragment screening reduces the demands on the mass spectrometer with respect to absolute throughput, detection limit, and dynamic range. We reasoned that these somewhat relaxed analytical criteria would provide an opportunity to utilize an open-source hardware/software approach [
38
,
39
] to circumvent the high cost, proprietary, and manufacture-specific nature of commercial mass spectrometry screening systems. Our platform is based on rapid hardware/software prototyping and comprises automated pick-up of protein-ligand conjugates from well-plates followed by injection onto parallelized dual desalting columns integrated with electrospray ionization for mass spectrometry detection. The system is operated through a simple Python graphical user interface running on microcontroller boards and agnostically integrates with diverse liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry instruments through a simple contact closure. To facilitate broad adoption [
40
], we provide a detailed parts manifest, production and assembly instructions, as well as software for instrument operation and data analysis. The system enables a primary screen throughput of ~10,000 covalent fragments per day in pooled format. As a powerful proof-of-concept, we screened purified UCHL1 against a library of 4200 covalent fragments and identified 41 hits. We re-screened these fragments as singletons and validated 27 of them as UCHL1 covalent binders. Through a series of orthogonal biochemical and chemoproteomic validation assays we identified 5 fragments that inhibited UCHL1 enzymatic activity and modified the catalytic cysteine residue. Our lead compound exhibited dose-dependent binding for UCHL1 with good selectivity across endogenous DUBs by activity-based protein profiling.

The inhibitory activity of each covalent hit fragment on UCHL1 was evaluated using the ubiquitin rhodamine 110 kinetic assay. All assays were performed at 2 nM UCHL1 and 200 nM ubiquitin rhodamine 110 (Boston Biochem) in 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, and 0.02 % Tween20 in 384-well plates (Corning). The assay was initiated with the addition of ubiquitin rhodamine 110. Kinetic fluorescence data were collected every 30 s over a 30-min period (excitation and emission at 480 nm and 535 nm, respectively) on a BMG LABTECH CLARIOstar Microplate Reader. Initial velocities (RFU/min) were extracted and plotted against Log[fragment, μM]. IC
50
values were derived using GraphPad Prism (non-linear regression: log(inhibitor) vs. response (three parameters)). Initially, fragments were tested on an eight-point dose-response curve (3.13–200 μM) with a two-hour incubation with UCHL1 at room temperature, with the assay repeated two times for each fragment (
n
= 2). Inhibitory compounds were then re-analyzed with twelve-point dose-response curves (400 nM - 400 μM) each repeated four times (
n
= 4), except for Z203045204 which was re-analyzed over a range of 100 nM–600 μM (
n
= 4). SB-1-F22, “F22” is a positive control compound [
17
] and was analyzed over a range of 4 nM–4 μM.
2.7.
In vitro target engagement
UCHL1 protein in PBS was incubated with each covalent fragment at the indicated concentration for 2 h at room temperature and then coincubated with a 10-fold molar excess of ubiquitin activity probe (ABP; 1:1 mix of biotin-Ub-PA and biotin-Ub-VME; UbiQ, Amsterdam, Netherlands) for 2 h at room temperature. Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and visualized by Coomassie staining. Gels were imaged on a Bio Rad Gel Doc XR+ (white epi illumination, white light conversion screen, 60 s exposure). Signal for Ub-ABP bound UCHL1 relative to DMSO control was determined by densitometry with ImageJ software [
43
]. Blockage was calculated as 1-(signal treated ABP-UCHL1/signal DMSO ABP-UCHL1) × 100 %.
2.8.
Middle-down proteomics
UCHL1 (1 μg) was incubated with covalent fragment (typically 3–25 μM) for between 2 and 16 h. Protein–fragment reactions were diluted with an equal volume of 8 M urea/50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, treated with 100 ng endoproteinase AspN (Promega, Madison, WI) for ~15 min at 37C, and then quenched with 10 % formic acid. N-terminal and C-terminal fragments from UCHL1 were loaded on onto a self-packed column (5 cm 50R2 packed into 500 μm PEEK tubing) and eluted using an HPLC gradient (0–100 % B in 1 min, A = 0.2 M acetic acid, B = 0.2 M acetic acid in acetonitrile) and subjected to CID MS/MS on a 7600 Zeno-Tof mass spectrometer (AB-Sciex) with a spray voltage of 5.5 kV. The mass spectrometer acquired MS1 scans and targeted CID MS/MS scans for labeled peptides (CE typically 15–25 eV, unit resolution). UCHL1/UCHL3 mixed reaction assay
UCHL1 and UCHL3 (1 μg each) were mixed and diluted with PBS to a final concentration of 1 μM, reacted with indicated compounds for 2 h at room temperature, and analyzed by LC–MS. Stoichiometry of UCHL1 was assessed from the peak height of doubly labeled protein, as middle down MS experiments indicated the second labeling event occupied the catalytic cysteine.
2.10.
Spectral library construction
A DUB-specific spectral library was generated from several independent samples of ABPP-enriched DUBs (protocol below) using HEK293 cell extracts. Following trypsin digestion, the peptides were analyzed using an optimized data-independent acquisition method on a tims-TOF Flex2 instrument. The spectral library was generated in DIA-NN (1.8.2 beta 8) using a library-free approach. The following search parameters were used: MS1 accuracy: 15 ppm, MS2 accuracy: 10 ppm, fixed carbamidomethylation of cysteines (+57.02146), variable oxidation of methionines (+15.9949), variable modification of cysteines with the tryptic remnants of the ubiquitin vinyl ester and ubiquitin propargyl amide probes (+172.085, +112.064 respectively). N-terminus methionine excision was enabled along with unrestricted digestion C-terminal of arginine and lysine residues, allowing 2 missed cleavages. Additional parameters were specified as follows: minimum fragment
m/z
set to 200, maximum fragment
m/z
set to 1800, minimum peptide length set to 6, maximum peptide length set to 40, minimum precursor
m/z
set to 300, maximum precursor
m/z
set to 1800, minimum precursor charge set to 2 and maximum precursor charge set to 6. Library precursors were reannotated using a FASTA database of human sequences downloaded from UniProt on 2023-08-10 appended to common contaminants. Only spectral matches with a
q
-value <0.01 were retained.
2.11.
Activity-based protein profiling
Pellets of HEK293T cells were lysed with 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5 % NP-40, 10 % glycerol and the lysate was clarified by centrifugation (14,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C). Protein concentration was measured by BCA and aliquots of extract were treated with indicated compounds for 4 h at room temperature. An equal mixture of ubiquitin activity probes (ABP; Ub-PA/VME; 50 μM probe/mg protein; UbiQ, Amsterdam, Netherlands) was then added and allowed to react for 15 min at room temperature. Magnetic streptavidin beads (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA) were added to capture proteins bound by the ABP and washed with PBS/0.2 % SDS to reduce the level of non-specifically bound proteins. Enriched proteins were then eluted with hexafluoroisopropanol. Eluted proteins were digested on STRAP micro columns (Protifi, Long Island, NY) according to the manufacturer instructions. Peptides were loaded onto EVO tips (Odense, Denmark) according to the manufacturer instructions and analyzed with a 20-SPD method on an EVO Sep One (column = 75 μm I.D. packed with 15 cm 1.5 μm Dr. Maisch C18 [ESI Source Solutions, Woburn, MA] with integrated emitter tip [
44
]) coupled to a Bruker timsTOF Flex2 mass spectrometer operated in DIA mode. For each compound, triplicates of each treatment (0, 5, 10, and 25 μm) for 2 independent experiments were analyzed (
n
= 6). Data files were processed with DIA-NN version 1.8.2 beta 8 using a custom spectral library of DUBs (see ‘
Spectral Library Construction
’ above). Other DIA-NN search settings were the same as above, except that MS1 and MS2 mass accuracies were set to auto-inference. After filtering DIA-NN results for precursors with intensity >1000, differential abundance analysis was performed using MS-DAP [
45
], using default settings (
https://github.com/ftwkoopmans/msdap
) with filter_min_peptide_per_prot = 2, dea_qvalue_threshold =0.05, and diffdetect_min _peptides_observed = 3. Heat maps were generated with Python 3.12 and show values for blockage > 50 % and
q

3.
Results
Fig. 1
highlights major hardware/software components along with user-input and performance criteria for our open source, medium-throughput covalent screening platform. We obtained libraries of commercial electrophilic compounds from Enamine (3200 compounds) and Chemdiv (1000 compounds), >70 % of which were selective for cysteine residues (
Supplementary Fig. 5
). We wrote a Python app (CreateScreenPools.py,
Fig. 1
top, left) to distribute covalent fragments first by warhead (33 bins,
Supplementary Table 3
), and then into pools of ≤ five compounds with sufficient mass separation (~10 Da, accounting for leaving groups) to enable deconvolution of target-fragment binding on low-resolution mass spectrometers. We further annotated each compound entry in CreateScreenPools.py with its associated SMILES string to ensure that chemical structure is tracked and incorporated into the final screen report. For the screen reported herein, the pool plates comprised 855 pools across 3 × 384 well plates distributed as follows: 1) acrylamides and cyanoacrylamides, 2) chloroacetamides, chloropropylamides, and chloroketones, 3) other warheads (
Supplementary Table 3
). Next, we used a Beckman i7 liquid handler to dispense target protein across matching wells and dispense pool plate compounds. After 2 h, each reaction plate was quenched with formic acid and frozen until mass spectrometry analysis.
To achieve a primary screen throughput of at least 10,000 fragments per day, we assembled a gantry style autosampler with x-y actuators to position well-plates below a sampling needle mounted on the z-axis actuator. The syringe alternated delivery of samples from each well into one of two identical flow paths comprising a sample loop and reversed phase microcapillary column which are parallelized across multiple 2- and 10 position, multi-port valves. The terminal valve serves to direct column eluent to the mass spectrometer electrospray interface. Standard pressure liquid chromatography pumps provide solvent flow for sample loading and desalting as well as organic gradient for elution of protein-ligand conjugates from the reversed phase columns. We wrote RobotControl.py deployed on a Raspberry pi 3.0 to calibrate syringe position as a function of well-plate geometry (number and depth of wells), control sample pick-up and delivery, and trigger LC gradient and mass spectrometer acquisition via contact closure. Another Python script (SmpListWizard.py) was executed on the mass spectrometer instrument computer to automatically create file names based on output from CreateScreenPools.py and then use these to populate the sample acquisition queue. This platform configuration enabled interleaved sample injection, de-salting, and ballistic 24 s organic gradient delivery across parallel flow paths to achieve LC–MS acquisition of intact protein mass spectra in 37 s. per well, corresponding to 2335 injections (11,675 fragments) in 24 h. Finally, we wrote FragmentScreen.py to automate processing of native mass spectrometry data files to identify potential fragment binding. Results are provided in PowerPoint slides for manual inspection or figure creation as well as excel/csv to support programmatic integration with other structural, SAR, or chemi-informatic tools.
We first sought to assess the speed, reproducibility, and carryover of our autosampler mass spectrometry system. Towards this end we arrayed 3 purified proteins (cytochrome c, enolase, and UCHL1) across 192 wells, (64 wells each) of a 384-well plate, along with 192 PBS blanks. Each protein (25 ng/μL) was injected in a volume of 40 μL (1 μg protein) followed by injection from a blank well. Consistent with our design and timing estimates, completion of 384 injections required just under 4 h of analysis time.
Fig. 2
(left) shows representative spectra for intact mass of each protein with violin plots (right) of summed peak intensity for each protein and blank injection. CVs for protein injections were <15 % with carryover <1 % in the blank injections. These results confirm the throughput, reproducibility, and low carryover of our open-source screening platform.
Having established baseline analytical performance for our screening platform we turned to our target of interest, ubiquitin c-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1). UCHL1 is a small (~28 kDa) well-structured cysteine protease DUB comprising multiple alpha-helices and beta sheets, a catalytic triad, as well as five other cysteine residues (
Fig. 3A
). Although UCHL1 has potential oncogenic activity in multiple cancers, existing small molecule inhibitors show disparate performance. For example, early-generation UCHL1 inhibitors LDN57444 [
46
], LDN91946 [
47
] and Z-VAE(OMe)-fmk [
48
] are now recognized to lack cellular target engagement and/or exhibit poor selectivity which limits their utility as chemical probes. More recently, cyanamide [
17
,
20
–
22
,
49
] (primarily cyanopyrrolidine) and chloroacetohydrazide [
19
] inhibitors of UCHL1 have been described (see
Table 1
for representative structures). While these compounds have been useful in some cell-based assays, none have progressed to in vivo studies potentially due to chemical or metabolic liabilities. Moreover, these compounds have not been uniformly tested for their off-target activity. These gaps motivated our interest to discover new chemical starting points for UCHL1.
Before initiating the library screen, we analyzed UCHL1 treated with DMSO (negative control) or the previously reported inhibitor SB-1-F22 [
17
] (positive control). From this pilot screen we determined the Z’-factor to be 0.75, indicating that our platform can reliably identify UCHL1 covalent hit-fragments [
50
]. For the library screen, we prepared reaction plates as described above, comprising 855 fragment pools, each incubated in a 12.5-fold molar excess (12.5 μM) with 1 μg of UCHL1 for 2 h at room temperature. Reactions were quenched with 1 % formic acid and analyzed directly from each reaction plate as described above using RobotControl.py and SmpListWizard.py.
Native mass spectrometry data files (.RAW) were directly processed using Fragment Screening.py that leverages the multiplierz toolkit [
42
] to read raw mass spectrometry data files. For each injection the average mass spectrum was extracted from the primary LC elution peak and deconvoluted with Unidec [
41
] to yield intact mass of UCHL1 along with signals for fragment-labeled and potential multi-labeled UCHL1. The script also provides an estimate of the binding stoichiometry, allowing prioritization of fragments. As illustrated in
Fig. 3B
, in the primary screen of pooled fragments we identified 41 compounds with binding stoichiometry ≥35 % (see
Supplementary Table 4
). Most ‘hit’ fragments were cyanoacrylamides (63 %), followed by chloroacetamides (21 %), a few chloroketones, and one acrylamide.
Fig. 3C
and
D
show deconvoluted spectra output by Fragmentscreening.py. The colored vertical lines indicate unlabeled UCHL1 along with calculated masses for UCHL1 labeled with each fragment in the pool. Peaks at higher masses suggest possible multi-labeling by one or more of the fragments. These spectra are packaged into PowerPoint slides, providing a convenient way to visually assess the credibility of top hits from the Excel report.
We validated hit fragments by incubating individual compounds at a reduced 6.25-fold molar excess (6.25 μM) with UCHL1. Consistent with lower compound concentration we set a minimum threshold of 15 % binding stoichiometry. Indeed, 39 of 41 fragments passed this step, corresponding to a validation rate >95 % for the primary screen. Moreover, at the reduced concentration, 11 fragments exhibited predominantly mono-labeling. For the remining 28 hits, we performed serial dilutions to identify 16 fragments which exhibited mono-labeling at ~3 μM. In total, these secondary screens validated a set of 27 hit-fragments suitable for subsequent characterization across orthogonal assays.
To test for inhibitory activity, we employed ubiquitin rhodamine 110 as a substrate in a kinetic assay (
Fig. 4A
) [
51
,
52
]. Of the 27 compounds tested, six inhibited UCHL1 with IC
50
values <25 μM (
n
= 4) and three at <10 μM (
n
= 4). Interestingly, Z203045204 and Z56871617 (IC
50
3.7 and 14 μM), contain a benzothiazole adjacent to the electrophile, which may mediate reversible interactions proximal to the catalytic triad to position the warhead for covalent modification of the catalytic cysteine (C90). The remaining fragments, including all the cyanoacrylamides, exhibited no inhibitory activity (IC
50
values >25 μM), or did not achieve maximum inhibition at the highest dose (
Supplementary Table 5
) and were removed from further consideration. To evaluate the inhibitory mechanism-of-action, we first used a ubiquitin activity-based probe (Ub-ABP) with purified UCHL1 to assess target engagement by SDS-PAGE for each hit compound (
Fig. 4B
). We observed dose dependent blocking of ABP binding (>50 % at 50 μM) for 5 validated hit-fragments, including benzothiazole core compounds Z203045204 and Z56871617 (
Fig. 4C
, full gels available in
Supplementary Data 1
). To confirm site(s) of fragment binding and stoichiometry, we utilized middle down mass spectrometry. We first established limited digestion conditions with the endoprotease Asp-N that yielded two UCHL1 peptides—an N-terminal 16.3 kDa peptide containing C52, C90 (catalytic cys), and C132 and an 8.9 kDa C-terminal peptide containing C152, C201, and C220 (
Fig. 4D
). Subsequent collision induced dissociation on a quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer was used to quantify covalent labeling at each cysteine residue on the two UCHL1 peptides after a 2 h treatment with compound. Consistent with the biochemical assays, we found that all 5 fragments covalently modified the UCHL1 catalytic cysteine residue C90 (
Fig. 4E
). Interestingly, they also labeled C152, the “bridge” or “cross-over” cysteine contained in a nearby disordered loop. This cysteine has been proposed to serve as a redox sensor [
53
] to protect the catalytic residue. To further explore fragment reactivities with C90 and C152, Z203045204 and Z56871617 were reacted at a lower concentration (3 μM) at short (2 h) and long (16 h) time points. C152 was modified first (2 h) and the catalytic residue (C90) was labeled after further incubation (16 h,
Fig. 4F
).
To examine selectivity of these compounds toward other UCHL family members, we reacted each of the 5 validated fragments with an equimolar mixture of UCHL-1 and UCHL-3 and evaluated the stoichiometry of labeling (
Fig. 5A
). The two chloroacetamide compounds—Z203045204 and Z56871617, exhibited strong selectivity for UCHL1. In fact, these compounds showed no reaction with UCHL3 at concentrations up to 50 μM. In contrast, the remaining 3 chloroketone compounds showed high levels of reactivity to both DUBs. Encouraged by the in vitro binding profiles of Z203045204 and Z56871617, we turned to activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) with mass spectrometry to assess the binding selectivity of both compounds against endogenous DUBs in a near-physiological context. Z56871617 showed no activity against any of the 57 DUBs reproducibly quantified at concentrations up to 25 μM (data not shown), while Z203045204 displaced the Ub-ABP (>50 %) from UCHL1 in a dose-dependent manner at 10 and 25 μM. Notably, Z203045204 was not active against sub-family members UCHL3 or UCHL5, and exhibited binding to BAP1, as well as USP5, USP8, and USP37/38, only at the highest concentration. Collectively, these results demonstrate a favorable selectivity profile for electrophilic fragment Z203045204 and suggest that it may serve as a useful starting point for future chemical optimization towards a covalent UCHL1 inhibitor.
4.
Discussion
Covalent inhibitors have often been developed by structure-guided elaboration of an existing reversible ligand with an electrophilic warhead (‘ligand-first’) [
54
–
56
]. More recently, an ‘electrophile-first’ strategy, whereby covalent fragment libraries are screened to identify an initial binder, followed by chemical elaboration to build selectivity, has come to the fore [
25
,
28
,
57
]. Mass spectrometry is particularly well-suited for characterization of covalent compound-protein adduct [
16
,
26
,
58
]. The Agilent Rapid Fire SPE-MS platform [
59
] is well-established as a ‘go-to’ system for high-throughput LC–MS screening applications, with inject-to-inject time of ~15 s per sample. Recently, higher throughput systems based on acoustic ejection [
60
] and IR-MALDESI [
61
] have also been reported. However, in contrast to typical diversity libraries, electrophilic fragment collections span broad chemical space with a comparatively modest number of compounds. As a result, target-based screens with covalent fragment libraries can be productively executed with medium-throughput approaches. Given these criteria we saw an opportunity to leverage open hardware principles [
38
–
40
,
62
–
64
] to assemble a fit-for-purpose mass spectrometry-based platform for covalent fragment screening that would reduce costs while increasing design, operational, and data analysis transparency. Towards this goal we used a combination of readily available and economical extruded aluminum and 3D printed construction elements, general-use precision motorized components, commodity microcontroller boards, and raspberry Pi microcomputers, to build a parallelized sample injection system to support rapid analysis (<40 s/sample) of intact protein-ligand conjugates by LC–MS. As described herein our system does rely on a commercial mass spectrometer and HPLC pumps; however, we intentionally chose systems that are unequivocally on the low end of the performance (and therefore cost) scale by current standards in chemoproteomics. We further provide software tools to facilitate pooling of library compounds, generation and management of target-compound reactions and filenames for intact protein mass spectrometry analysis, as well as automated processing of screening data. Consistent with open hardware and software principles, we provide (through the
supplementary materials
) extensive and standardized hardware design and assembly documentation. This information includes openSCAD files for 3D printed components, detailed parts list, build instructions, and operation manual. We also provide Python and other code specific for the screening platform as well as links to our and others’ open source software tools that support analysis of fragment screening data. Importantly, results are output in human- and machine-readable formats and include information for compound structures. In this way our screening data is immediately interoperable with other chemi-informatics analysis tools like DataWarrior [
65
] or RDKit [
66
].
Open hardware design seeks to improve design and operational transparency while reducing the costs associated with advanced scientific instruments and workflows. These are conceptually laudable goals and can help democratize access to what are otherwise proprietary and expensive technologies. However, in practice widespread adoption of this paradigm requires that practitioners can leverage these benefits to achieve actionable results comparable to purpose-built commercial platforms. With a throughput of ~10,000 compounds per day, our platform readily supports target-based screens against electrophilic fragment libraries. Indeed, covalent fragment screens performed on the commercial [
59
] and research [
60
,
61
] platforms noted above are also in the range of 3000–10,000 covalent compounds. The number of fragments notwithstanding, one potential advantage of the higher throughput offered by these recently reported systems is the ability to analyze compounds individually and hence complete the primary screen in approximately the same time as a pooled format screen. As a powerful proof-of-performance we executed a covalent fragment screen against UCHL1, a DUB that has been nominated as a therapeutic target in neurodegenerative disease and cancer. Primary and secondary screens performed on our open hardware platform yielded 27 UCHL1 covalent binders. Of these, we validated 5 hits that inhibited enzyme activity (IC
50
<25 μM), blocked the binding of a Ubiquitin-ABP (≥50 %), and covalently modified the catalytic cysteine (C90). Two of these compounds (Z203045204 and Z56871617) exhibited no binding in in vitro experiments with the closely related family member UCHL3 at concentrations up to 50 μM. And in ABPP experiments performed in cell extracts, only Z203045204 blocked binding of the ubiquitin probe to UCHL1 and otherwise showed excellent selectivity for a primary screening hit across 57 endogenous DUBs. Indeed, our success in prosecuting hits from the primary screen through a series of orthogonal validation assays to nominate Z203045204 as a promising starting point for a UCHL1 inhibitor credentials the fit-for-purpose performance of our open hardware platform. Moreover, our ability to validate cyanoacrylamide compounds as primary hits demonstrates that our platform is generally suitable for screening reversible-covalent fragments [
67
]. Beyond validation of UCHL1 binding in the primary screen, we note that none of the cyanoacrylamide hit compounds showed evidence of inhibitory activity by the Ub-Rho or target engagement biochemical assays. While beyond the scope of this report, it will be interesting in future studies to explore whether the cysteine(s) modified by these reversible-covalent compounds reside in novel pockets which could be leveraged for development of recruiter or other novel mechanism-of-action modalities.
